ety.text: The verb is derived from Middle English ridden (“to remove debris, obstructions, etc., from (a place), to clear; to complete (something unfinished); to free (someone or something); to relieve (someone); etc.”), probably from Old English *ryddan (“to remove debris, obstructions, etc., from (a place), to clear”) (the past participle form ġeryd is attested), from Proto-Germanic *riudijaną (“to clear”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hrewdʰ- (“to clear land”), or possibly from *Hrew- (“to dig out, tear out; to open; to acquire”).
The adjective is derived from rid, the obsolete past participle form of ride.

senses.d: Followed by of: to free (oneself or someone, or a place) from an annoyance or hindrance.
ex: I’m glad to be rid of that stupid nickname.
We’re trying to rid the world of poverty.

senses.d: Followed by away, from, or out of: to remove (oneself or someone, or something, that is annoying, troublesome, or unwanted).
ex: [G]old he vvill giue her, / Theſe vvill I make induction to her ruine, / And rid ſhame from my houſe, griefe from my heart […]

senses.d: Often followed by from, of, or out of: to free or release, or to rescue or save, (oneself or someone, or something).
To clear (a place or way); especially, to clear (land) of trees, undergrowth, etc.
Sometimes followed by away: to destroy or kill (someone).
ex: This Gloſter ſhould be quickly rid the VVorld, / To rid vs from the feare vve haue of him.
The furious Tybalt caſt an enuious thruſt [of the rapier], / That rid the life of ſtout Mercutio.

senses.d: Sometimes followed by up: to remove obstacles or refuse from (a place); to clean, to clear out; specifically, to clear or empty (the stomach).
Followed by up: to eradicate (something); to root out, to uproot.
Sometimes followed by away or off: to complete or get through (a task, or work).
ex: [T]he Printer, in one day ſhall rid / More Books, then yerſt a thouſand VVrighters did.

senses.d: Often followed by up: to put (a place, such as a room or a table) in order; to clear, to tidy.
ex: The four breakfasted by the thin light, and the ‘house-ridding’ was taken in hand.

senses.d: To dismiss (someone) who has attended on a person; (reflexive) to remove (oneself) from a person's presence after attending to them.
ex: We be able ynough to rydde vs of this mater without the [thee]: […]
[A] Judge riddeth a perſone aunſweryng before hym to the lawe at the barre.

senses.d: Chiefly of a place: which has been ridded (etymology 1, verb sense 1.4.1) or cleared; rid-up.
ex: We will make room for you! We will make a rid road from here to Winchester!
